children.text: Chapter 5 begins by saying that FHIR interoperability, AI clinical governance and cybersecurity are three implementation risks that any organization building on a data infrastructure foundation will meet, in roughly that order, as the foundation comes online. A standards mandate without governance produces ungoverned clinical AI. A connected, data-rich system without security produces a larger attack surface. The order is a planning principle and not a calendar, and this lesson turns it into one.

It uses the chapter's implementation matrix, six investments with indicative cost, time to value, return crossover and Vermont benchmarks, and the chapter's headline sequencing concern: the analytics capability that must be in place before global budgets begin. The matrix figures are the book's indicative ranges, and the lesson asks the reader to replace them with quotes. The analytics status is drawn from public procurement listings and a state report, which show activity but no award.
The lesson ends with a method for building a three-year technology plan that respects dependencies and funding limits.
The Implementation Matrix

children.text: Read the matrix for its structure, not its precision. Three investments pay back quickly and cheaply: EHR optimization for structured data capture, which makes everything else work; access to the state claims platform; and cybersecurity assessment, whose return is risk avoidance from the start. Three pay back slowly: FHIR and API development at 18 to 24 months to crossover, clinical AI at 12 to 24 months and shared analytics at 36 to 48 months. The cheap ones are prerequisites for the expensive ones, which suggests an order.

The ranges are the chapter's indicative figures, 'indicative ranges' in its words, and actual costs vary with the organization's size, existing infrastructure and approach. They should be replaced with vendor quotes before they enter a budget, and the finance course's guidance on evidence applies: label each figure as assumption, published estimate, local estimate or measured result.
A Defensible Order

Combine the matrix with the dependencies from the earlier tracks. Start with data capture and security, because they are cheap, quick and underlie the rest: structured data capture makes the FHIR interface worth connecting to, and a security baseline reduces the risk of everything that follows. Add identity, the master patient index of Track 1, before provider-to-provider exchange. Build the FHIR interfaces for patient access and provider query next, then prepare for the payer APIs due in 2027. Put the AI governance framework in place before the first clinical AI deployment, not afterward, and adopt decision support design principles before adding alerts.

Shared analytics comes last in elapsed time not because it matters least but because it depends on the others: it needs clean data, identity and exchange. It also has the longest payback, so a network that starts late will not have it when it is needed. That tension, between a long lead time and a dependency on earlier work, is the sequencing problem the chapter identifies.

children.text: The Analytics Gap Before Global Budgets

Chapter 5 opens by calling the sequencing vulnerability the analytics vendor gap that must close before global budgets take effect in fiscal year 2028. Chapter 3 repeats the warning, saying the Agency of Human Services and Green Mountain Care Board analytics vendor procurement should be treated as a critical-path decision with a hard deadline, because Vermont cannot repeat at the system level the experience of organizations assuming financial risk without analytics to manage it.

The public record this lesson could find shows activity, not an award. The Board's website lists a data analytics solicitation among closed requests awaiting award, seeking vendors for health care expenditure and ad hoc analyses, though the page is undated. A March 2026 state report on health care system transformation says funds remain for a contractor to provide analytics supporting regional plans that will inform the Strategic Plan, and that this contract was under negotiation. A May 2026 request for proposals issued by the Agency of Digital Services for the Board concerns modernizing the Board's data infrastructure, including configuring its environment within the Statewide Data Lake. Hospital pricing and budget data standardization solicitations were posted in early 2026. None of the results showed a named award.

The fair reading is that procurement is under way and that its completion date is not known from the sources read. For a hospital that is exactly the situation to plan around. If the state tool arrives late or incomplete, the hospital's own analytics, and the network's, are what stand between it and a budget set without the information it needs.
When a critical dependency's date is uncertain, plan a version of your own that does not wait for it, even if it is smaller.
Funding the Plan

The funding sources the chapter names are Rural Health Transformation grants, which Vermont's program reportedly allocates at $195 million a year for five years, with information technology investments including cybersecurity and shared analytics, and the hospital's own operating budget. The political sustainability course's operating-funding test applies: for each investment, who pays in year three? Grants can fund the build. They rarely fund the maintenance, licensing and staffing that keep an interface or a monitoring service alive.

A technology plan should therefore show two budgets side by side: the build cost by year and the recurring cost that begins when each element goes live. The recurring costs are what a board must be asked to accept. Showing them at the start avoids the surprise, a year after a grant-funded launch, that the program needs $400,000 a year to keep running.

children.text: One more discipline helps: review the plan each quarter against what actually happened. Compare planned and actual dates, spending and measures of use, and ask whether the sequence still makes sense. Plans drift, and a review that notices drift early costs far less than one that finds it at the end of a funding period.
Risks to the Sequence

Any three-year plan meets interruptions. A vendor slips a release that the payer APIs depend on. The one staff member who understood the interface leaves. A grant is delayed or cut. A security incident forces the team to redirect months of effort. A sequencing plan should therefore name its critical path, the chain of dependent items that determines the end date, and its single points of failure, whether people, vendors or funds. Protect the critical path first: cross-train the staff, write down the interface documentation and hold contingency in the schedule.

It also helps to define decision points where the plan can change. If the identity service is not ready by a stated date, provider query is postponed and the team works on payer API readiness instead. If the state's analytics contract is not awarded by a stated date, the network builds its minimum viable analytics. Writing the rule in advance avoids a debate about whether to slip when a delay becomes visible, and it keeps effort from stalling behind a dependency that is out of the organization's hands.

points: Chapter 5 says FHIR, AI governance and cybersecurity are three implementation risks met in roughly that order as a data foundation comes online.

The matrix's quick, cheap investments, structured data capture, claims platform access and a security assessment, are prerequisites for the slower ones: FHIR and APIs, clinical AI and shared analytics.
Matrix cost ranges are the book's indicative figures; replace them with quotes and label each by its evidence rung.
A defensible order starts with security, data capture and identity, then builds exchange, adds governance before AI deployment and finishes with shared analytics.

The analytics vendor gap before fiscal year 2028 global budgets is the chapter's headline sequencing risk; public listings show solicitations and a contract under negotiation but no award in the sources read.
When a critical dependency's date is uncertain, plan a smaller version that does not wait for it.
Show build cost and recurring cost side by side, and answer who pays in year three before accepting grant funding.
